PROTOTYPES / FIRST LESSONS

Every teacher.
Something to teach.

A first encounter with each subject: a clear explanation, a worked demonstration and a chance to show understanding. These introductory lesson proposals establish the teaching content behind the characters.

THE DEVELOPED EXAMPLE

Music begins
with listening.

Unit 1.1 introduces sound, noise, pitch, loudness, duration and timbre through Soundscape Mapping and an instrument comparison.

EnglishMathScienceHistoryGeographyLanguage ArtsHealthPhysical EducationArtDramaTechnology

01 / ENGLISH

Beholder

Word choice & connotation

THE TEACHER EXPLAINS
Explain how words can name a similar action while suggesting different attitudes.
A WORKED DEMONSTRATION
Compare “walked,” “strode” and “crept” in the same arrival sentence. Explain how each verb changes what a reader imagines.
APPLICATION & UNDERSTANDING
Revise the sentence for a stated tone. Explain the implication of the chosen verb and point to the word that creates it.

02 / MATH

Yeti Wizard

Variables & rate of change

THE TEACHER EXPLAINS
Define an input, an output and a variable. Show how one rule can describe a whole set of related values.
A WORKED DEMONSTRATION
Work through y = 2n + 3 for n = 1, 2 and 3. Connect the outputs 5, 7 and 9 to a table and show why each input step adds two to the output.
APPLICATION & UNDERSTANDING
Calculate the output for n = 4, then explain why the change is two rather than three. Expected output: 11.

03 / SCIENCE

Chuul

Observation, inference & a fair test

THE TEACHER EXPLAINS
An observation describes evidence; an inference offers an explanation. A controlled comparison changes one selected variable while other relevant conditions are held constant.
A WORKED DEMONSTRATION
Separate “the leaf has brown spots” from “the plant has a disease.” Model a test of a proposed cause and name what would be changed and measured.
APPLICATION & UNDERSTANDING
Classify an observation and an inference. For the proposed test, identify one variable to change, an outcome to measure and a condition to keep constant.

04 / HISTORY

Displacer Beast

Sources & corroboration

THE TEACHER EXPLAINS
Explain how a source’s author, purpose and access to an event shape what it can tell us. Corroboration compares evidence across sources.
A WORKED DEMONSTRATION
Read a short diary account and public record of the same event. Model one supported claim and identify a question neither source settles.
APPLICATION & UNDERSTANDING
Support a claim with details from the sources. Explain one difference between the accounts and one uncertainty that remains.

05 / GEOGRAPHY

Ettin

Map scale & contour lines

THE TEACHER EXPLAINS
Scale relates distance on a map to distance on the ground. Contour lines connect points of equal elevation; closer spacing indicates a steeper slope when the contour interval is consistent.
A WORKED DEMONSTRATION
Use a map scale to estimate a route’s distance. Compare two routes and explain the elevation information shown by their contour lines.
APPLICATION & UNDERSTANDING
Estimate a new route’s distance and explain which section is steeper, citing the map scale and contour spacing.

06 / LANGUAGE ARTS

Brass Dragon

Audience, purpose & register

THE TEACHER EXPLAINS
Explain how a message’s purpose and intended reader influence its wording, detail and level of formality.
A WORKED DEMONSTRATION
Compare two messages asking for help: one addressed to a friend and one to a school administrator. Explain a deliberate wording and structure choice in each.
APPLICATION & UNDERSTANDING
Adapt a short message for a different audience. Identify one changed phrase and explain why it fits the new reader.

07 / HEALTH

Giant Spider

Evaluating health information

THE TEACHER EXPLAINS
Distinguish an unsupported claim from a claim supported by a traceable source. Explain how to ask who produced the information, what evidence it cites and whether the evidence supports the claim.
A WORKED DEMONSTRATION
Compare two prepared classroom messages. Follow a cited source and separate the message’s assertion from the evidence it actually supplies.
APPLICATION & UNDERSTANDING
Identify the claim and evidence in a new example. Explain what should be verified before accepting it; popularity alone does not establish accuracy.

08 / PHYSICAL EDUCATION

Gnoll

Specificity, overload & recovery

THE TEACHER EXPLAINS
Introduce three training principles: practice relates to the skill being developed; an appropriate increase in demand can stimulate adaptation; recovery is part of a training plan.
A WORKED DEMONSTRATION
Compare hypothetical schedules with stated training goals. Identify examples of specificity, a change in demand and planned recovery.
APPLICATION & UNDERSTANDING
Name the principle illustrated by a schedule and explain its relationship to the goal. This is analysis of examples, not a personal exercise prescription.

09 / ART

Oobleck

Contrast & visual hierarchy

THE TEACHER EXPLAINS
Explain how differences in value, size and placement guide attention through a composition. A focal point is the area a viewer is drawn to first.
A WORKED DEMONSTRATION
Show the same composition with one value or size relationship changed. Explain why the eye is drawn to a different area.
APPLICATION & UNDERSTANDING
Annotate or revise a simple composition. Identify its intended focal point and explain which visual relationship makes it stand out.

10 / DRAMA

Medusa

Objective & subtext

THE TEACHER EXPLAINS
A character’s objective is what they want in a scene. Subtext is the meaning or intention carried beneath the literal words.
A WORKED DEMONSTRATION
Read “You came back” twice with different intentions. Explain how pace, pitch and emphasis communicate each interpretation.
APPLICATION & UNDERSTANDING
Use details from one reading to explain its intention. Annotate how the line could be delivered with a different objective.

11 / TECHNOLOGY

Mimic

Algorithms, sequence & precision

THE TEACHER EXPLAINS
An algorithm is an ordered set of instructions for a task. Explain how ambiguous wording or the order of steps can change the result.
A WORKED DEMONSTRATION
Trace a short instruction sequence step by step. Show how an unclear instruction or misplaced step produces an unintended result.
APPLICATION & UNDERSTANDING
Trace a second sequence, identify a faulty instruction and rewrite it precisely. Explain how the correction changes the outcome.

THE HEADMASTER / LICH

How we explain
what we know.

The Lich introduces the school’s expectations for reasoning: make a claim, identify evidence and explain the connection between them.

She models a short evidence-supported explanation. Students then use supplied observations to support a conclusion and distinguish the conclusion from its evidence.

Practical orientation, including Pause and Help, is introduced separately from subject teaching.
